topics.name: unless / until / as soon as / no sooner ... than / hardly ... when

options: Although it was dark, but Neel walked home bravely.
Although it was dark, Neel walked home bravely.
Despite it was dark, Neel walked home bravely.
questions.rule: Although already joins the ideas, so don't add but. Despite cannot take a full clause.

options: Asha decided to face her fear.
Asha decided to faced her fear.
questions.rule: Decide is followed by the infinitive: to + base form - to face.

options: Do not give up until you will reach the top.
Do not give up until you reached the top.
Do not give up until you reach the top.
questions.rule: After until, use the simple present for a future event: until you reach.

options: Despite the heavy rain, the team kept playing.
Despite of the heavy rain, the team kept playing.
Despite the heavy rain, the team kept play.
questions.rule: Say despite (no 'of') or in spite of. Kept is followed by an -ing form.

options: The storm was fierce, but the sailors did not lost hope.
The storm was fierce, but the sailors did not lose hope.
The storm was fierce, although but the sailors did not lose hope.
questions.rule: A compound sentence joins two clauses with one linker like but; after did not, use the base form.

options: Facing problems calmly needs real courage.
Face problems calmly needs real courage.
Faced problems calmly needs real courage.
questions.rule: An action used as the subject takes the gerund (-ing form): Facing problems.

options: Unless you don't practise daily, you will not improve.
Unless you will practise daily, you will not improve.
Unless you practise daily, you will not improve.
questions.rule: Unless means 'if not', so don't add another not; use the simple present after it.

options: Hardly the sun had risen when the climbers set out.
Hardly had the sun risen than the climbers set out.
Hardly had the sun risen when the climbers set out.
questions.rule: Hardly takes inverted order (had the sun risen) and pairs with when.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: After a preposition like of, use the gerund: fond of climbing.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: A full clause (he was injured) needs Although; despite takes a noun or -ing form.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: After until, use the simple present for the future; Aai is singular, so comes.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: The relative clause tells a past event, matching was: who reached the top first.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Tanvi received the action, so use the past participle: Encouraged by her coach.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Every climber is singular, so use was. However after a semicolon links the ideas.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Yesterday and rose show the past, so use the simple past: began.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: No sooner always pairs with than; hardly pairs with when.

questions.after: the darkness, the boy was not afraid.
questions.rule: The darkness is a noun phrase, not a clause, so use Despite.
Hope is followed by the infinitive: hope to reach.

questions.after: your fear, it will control you.
questions.rule: After unless, use the simple present to talk about the future: unless you face.
The fixed phrase is in spite of + noun.

questions.after: the poet did not lose courage.
questions.rule: Yet joins two clauses into a compound sentence; despite can't join clauses and however needs a semicolon.
Avoid is followed by a gerund: avoid playing.

questions.before: Hardly had the climbers reached the camp
questions.rule: Hardly ... when is the correct pair (No sooner ... than).

questions.after: the poem twice, Isha understood its message.
questions.rule: The perfect participle Having read shows an action finished before the main one.
Want is followed by the infinitive: want to be.
Despite + noun phrase (heavy rain), then the main clause.
Until + simple present: until you reach home.
The relative clause who never gives up describes the girl.
No sooner had + subject + past participle ... than + simple past.

chat: What do you want to do after school?
options: I want to become a pilot.
I want to becoming a pilot.
questions.rule: Want is followed by to + base form: want to become.

chat: Did you go for your run this morning?
questions.rule: Although + clause (it was raining); despite cannot take a full clause.

chat: When should we start the warm-up?
options: As soon as everyone arrives, sir.
As soon as everyone will arrive, sir.
As soon as everyone arrived, sir.
questions.rule: For a future event after as soon as, use the simple present: arrives.

chat: Why didn't you join the trek, Om?
options: I had a sprained ankle; therefore, I stay back.
I had a sprained ankle; therefore, I stayed back.
I had a sprained ankle; therefore, I staying back.
questions.rule: Therefore gives the result; both parts are past: had ... stayed.

chat: How do you stay calm before exams?
options: By take deep breaths and plan my time.
By taking deep breaths and planning my time.
By to take deep breaths and planning my time.
questions.rule: After the preposition by, use gerunds: by taking ... and planning.

options: Yes, and I also helped Kiran, which was stuck.
Yes, and I also help Kiran, who was stuck yesterday.
Yes, and I also helped Kiran, who was stuck.
questions.rule: Use who for a person in a relative clause, and keep the past: helped.

chat: Will you come to the fair with us?
options: Yes, unless it will rain heavily.
Yes, unless it doesn't rain heavily.
questions.rule: Unless = if not, so no extra negative, and use the simple present: unless it rains.

chat: Why do you look so happy?
options: I'm proud of have finished my first marathon.
I'm proud of having finished my first marathon.
I'm proud to having finished my first marathon.
questions.rule: After proud of, use a gerund; having finished shows the action is complete.

questions.source: It was very dark, but Neha was not afraid.
options: Although it was very dark, Neha was not afraid.
Although it was very dark, but Neha was not afraid.
Although it was very dark, Neha were not afraid.
questions.rule: With although, drop but: one linker is enough.

questions.source: Although she was nervous, Tara sang on the stage.
options: Despite being nervous, Tara sang on the stage.
Despite she was nervous, Tara sang on the stage.
Despite of being nervous, Tara sang on the stage.
questions.rule: Despite + -ing form or noun (no 'of'): Despite being nervous.

questions.prompt: Join the sentences using an infinitive.
questions.source: Raj went to the hills. He wanted to see the sunrise.
options: Raj went to the hills for see the sunrise.
Raj went to the hills to see the sunrise.
Raj went to the hills to seeing the sunrise.
questions.rule: The infinitive to see shows purpose.

questions.prompt: Make it a simple sentence using a participle.
questions.source: He was brave, and he faced the storm.
options: Been brave, he faced the storm.
Being brave, he faced the storm.
Be brave, he faced the storm.
questions.rule: The participle Being brave replaces the first clause, leaving one finite verb.

questions.prompt: Make it a complex sentence using 'who'.
questions.source: Arjun lost a leg in an accident. He still climbed the mountain.
options: Arjun, who lost a leg in an accident, still climbed the mountain.
Arjun, which lost a leg in an accident, still climbed the mountain.
Arjun, who lost a leg in an accident, still climb the mountain.
questions.rule: Who introduces a clause about a person; the main verb stays past: climbed.

questions.source: If you do not believe in yourself, you will not win.
options: Unless you do not believe in yourself, you will not win.
Unless you will believe in yourself, you will not win.
Unless you believe in yourself, you will not win.
questions.rule: Unless = if not, so drop do not: Unless you believe.

questions.source: As soon as the sailors saw the light, they cheered.
options: Hardly the sailors had seen the light when they cheered.
Hardly had the sailors seen the light than they cheered.
Hardly had the sailors seen the light when they cheered.
questions.rule: Hardly had + subject + past participle ... when + simple past.

questions.source: The poet was brave. He was also hopeful.
options: The poet was not only brave but also hopeful.
The poet was not only brave and also hopeful.
The poet was not only brave but also hope.
questions.rule: Not only pairs with but also, joining two adjectives: brave and hopeful.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this message.
questions.rule: Wants to + base form (watch); spend time + -ing form (sitting).

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this message.
questions.rule: Despite goes before a noun (the heavy rain) or an -ing form (feeling tired).

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this message.
questions.rule: The story is in the past, so both verbs take the simple past: returned, started.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: Who for a person; in order to + base form (keep); a man who refuses (singular, present).

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: No sooner ... than; a clause (we were all frightened) needs Although; stayed ... and guided (both past).
